## Introduction

This vignette walks through a complete classification workflow with
`scorcher`. The task is to predict penguin species from a mix of numeric
measurements and categorical variables in the
[Palmer Penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/index.html)
dataset.

The example is intentionally small and concrete. It shows how to prepare a
tabular dataset, create tensors, define a graph, inspect the architecture,
train the model, audit the run, and evaluate accuracy on test data that was not
used for training. A tensor is the data format used by `torch`; for this
example, it is essentially a numeric matrix with a type attached.

<br>

<img src="https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/reference/figures/lter_penguins.png" alt="'Meet the Palmer penguins' Artwork by @allison_horst" width="100%">

## Setup

### Installing and Loading Required Packages

Before we begin, ensure that you have the necessary packages installed. You can install them using the following commands:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("ggimage")
install.packages("torch")
install.packages("scorcher")
install.packages("palmerpenguins")
```

Additionally, you'll need to install the system dependencies used by R `torch`.
Follow the R `torch` installation instructions
[here](https://torch.mlverse.org/start/installation/). Then load the packages
used in this analysis:

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggimage)
library(torch)
library(scorcher)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

### Loading the Data

We'll now load the Palmer Penguins dataset.

```{r}
data("penguins")

head(penguins) # Print the first few rows of the data
```

### Visualizing the Data

Let's visualize the dataset to better understand its structure and relationships.

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
# Visualizing the Palmer Penguins data

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
    geom_image(
      data = tibble(bill_length_mm = 35, bill_depth_mm = 10),
      aes(image = "https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/reference/figures/culmen_depth.png"), 
      size = 1) +
    theme_minimal() +
    geom_point(aes(color = species, shape = species), size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_smooth(aes(color = species, shape = species), method = "lm", se = FALSE) + 
    scale_color_manual(values = c("darkorange","purple","cyan4")) +
    ylim(c(10, 22.5)) +
    labs(title = "Bill length and depth",
         subtitle = "Dimensions for Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo Penguins at Palmer Station LTER",
         caption = "Artwork by @allison_horst",
         x = "Bill Length (mm)",
         y = "Bill Depth (mm)",
         color = "Species",
        shape = "Species") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  
```

### Data Preprocessing

For a neural network, every input needs to be numeric. The preprocessing below
removes incomplete rows, standardizes the continuous measurements, and encodes
categorical variables as integer levels.

```{r}

penguins <- penguins |>
  
  drop_na() |> # Removing rows with missing values for simplicity
  
  mutate( 
    across( # Normalizing numerical features
      c(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g),
      ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))
    ),
    across( # Encoding categorical features
      c(species, island, sex),
      ~ as.integer(as.factor(.x))
    )
  )

```

### Creating Training and Test Sets

Next, we'll split the data into training and test sets.

```{r}
set.seed(123)

train_indices <- sample(1:nrow(penguins), 0.8 * nrow(penguins))
train_data <- penguins[train_indices, ]
test_data <- penguins[-train_indices, ]
```

## Using Scorcher

### Defining the Neural Network

The model below uses the seven prepared predictors as input and returns three
class scores, one for each species. The largest score is the model's predicted
species. During training, cross-entropy loss compares those raw scores with the
correct species label and gives the model a number to reduce.

```{r}
# Create the dataloader

x_train <- torch_tensor(as.matrix(train_data[, -1]), dtype = torch_float())
y_train <- torch_tensor(as.integer(train_data$species), dtype = torch_long())

dl <- scorch_create_dataloader(x_train, y_train, batch_size = 32)

# Define the neural network

scorch_model <- initiate_scorch(dl) |>
  scorch_input(x) |>
  scorch_layer(linear, in_features = 7, out_features = 16) |>
  scorch_layer(relu) |>
  scorch_layer(linear, in_features = 16, out_features = 8) |>
  scorch_layer(relu) |>
  scorch_layer(linear, in_features = 8, out_features = 3, .name = species_scores) |>
  scorch_output()

plot(scorch_model, detail = "full", input_shapes = list(x = "batch x 7"))
```

### Training the Neural Network

Training combines the graph, loss function, optimizer, and dataloader. A
dataloader feeds the model small groups of rows at a time. Because the three
species are not perfectly balanced, the loss uses class weights computed from
the training set so that less common species still matter during training.

```{r}
# Define weights for imbalanced classes

weight <- length(train_data$species) /
  (3 * torch_stack(lapply(1:3, function(i) sum(train_data$species == i))))

weight <- weight$squeeze()

# Compile the neural network

scorch_model <- scorch_model |>
  compile_scorch(
    loss_fn          = nn_cross_entropy_loss(weight = weight),
    optimizer_fn     = optim_adam,
    optimizer_params = list(lr = 0.001)
  )

# Fit the neural network

scorch_model <- scorch_model |>
  fit_scorch(num_epochs = 200, verbose = TRUE)

run <- scorch_snapshot(
  scorch_model,
  data = list(features = x_train, labels = y_train),
  config = list(dataset = "palmerpenguins", epochs = 200)
)

scorch_audit(run)
autoplot(run, type = "history")
```

The same graph can be converted for use with `luz`. Use a regular torch
dataloader for `luz`, so each batch contains predictors and the correct species
labels.

```{r luz, eval=FALSE}
torch_module <- as_torch(scorch_model)
luz_dl <- torch::dataloader(
  torch::tensor_dataset(x_train, y_train),
  batch_size = 32,
  shuffle = TRUE
)

luz_fit <- torch_module |>
  luz::setup(
    loss = nn_cross_entropy_loss(),
    optimizer = optim_adam
  ) |>
  luz::fit(data = luz_dl, epochs = 200)
```

### Evaluating the Model

Evaluation uses the test set that was not used for training.
`scorch_evaluate()` switches the fitted model into evaluation mode, runs
prediction, and computes the requested metric.

```{r}
x_test <- torch_tensor(as.matrix(test_data[, -1]), dtype = torch_float())
y_test <- torch_tensor(as.integer(test_data$species), dtype = torch_long())

scorch_evaluate(
  scorch_model,
  input = x_test,
  truth = y_test,
  metric = "accuracy"
)
```

For a model trained with `luz`, use `luz::evaluate()` on a regular torch
dataloader:

```{r luz-evaluate, eval=FALSE}
luz_test_dl <- torch::dataloader(
  torch::tensor_dataset(x_test, y_test),
  batch_size = 32
)

luz::evaluate(luz_fit, data = luz_test_dl)

```

## Conclusion

This example showed the main steps for tabular classification with Scorcher:
prepare numeric data for `torch`, define the model graph, train by comparing
class scores with known labels, audit the run, and evaluate accuracy. The same
pattern can be adapted to other tabular classification problems by changing the
preprocessing, input dimension, and number of output classes.
